t: A spade leans against the throne, its blade still bright. The Barrow-King stands between you and it.
The mud here has been heaped up and patted down, and the reeds will not grow on it. Something is buried under there.
You have a spade. Take it in your hands first.
You need a spade to dig this up. Maybe find one.
Marta's bed. Her money box sleeps under that pillow; she would not thank you for lying on it.
Marta's bed. Her money box sleeps under that pillow; she would not thank you for lying on it.
The blanket is rough but warm. How long do you sleep?
You wake with a start. The hearth has burned down to embers and the window is black.
Outside, something heavy crashes against the fence. A laugh, low and ugly, and a second voice hushing it. Then the crunch of splintering wood.
Outside, something heavy crashes against the fence. A laugh, low and ugly, and a second voice hushing it. Then the crunch of splintering wood.
Someone is in the yard. Your pitchfork leans against the wall outside, by the door.
Someone is in the yard. Your pitchfork leans against the wall outside, by the door.
We have done our business, you and I. Forget my face.
He watches you from under his hood and says nothing.
Travelling light? Wise. The roads have ears.
The man in grey looks at your pack, then at the village behind you.
The old man has read it, then.
He shrugs.
Paper can still burn. People too. Good day.
A sensible soul.
The coins are cold. By the time you look up, the road is empty.
Then may Dunhollow bury you with it.
He steps back into the trees.
For a moment something like a smile.
I carry nothing for anyone. Thirty-five.
A thin man in a grey cloak steps out from behind the hedge. His boots are too clean for the road.
You carry a letter sealed with a B. My master would pay handsomely to have it back, unread by village elders. Thirty-five copper. More than those farmers will ever give you.
She looks at you a long moment.
Huh. There are still some of you left.
She drops a small pouch at your feet.
For the road. And watch the man in grey.
You receive 10 copper.
Smart.
She tosses the purse.
Tell the old man we were too many.
You receive 25 copper.
A woman in mail rises from beside the fire, morningstar resting on her shoulder. The others reach for their blades; she waves them down.
She squints.
An elf, running Hamond's errands? The Baron would pay good silver for ears like yours. Lucky for you I don't work for him on Sundays.
Hamond's errand-runner. Before you swing that thing: my people were colliers in these woods until the Baron burned us out. Now we rob for him, because he pays and nobody else does.
So. You can bleed for an old man's village. Or you can walk away twenty-five copper richer. Or, if you have a heart in there, let us leave this valley tonight and never come back.
They squirm and nip all the way. Marta will know what to do.
Where Old Greymaw fell, you hear a thin whimper. Under the roots of a fallen pine: three wolf pups, eyes barely open, pressed against each other.
Where Old Greymaw fell, you hear a thin whimper. Under the roots of a fallen pine: three wolf pups, eyes barely open, pressed against each other.
They are too small to survive alone. And far too small to be dangerous. For now.
She throws the soup at the wall of the well-house. Then she sits down very slowly.
You let me warm his supper for weeks.
A long silence.
Go away. …No. Stay a moment. Then go away.
Ada is setting a bowl of soup on the well's edge, beside a spoon nobody will use.
Ada is setting a bowl of soup on the well's edge, beside a spoon nobody will use.
You tell her. The city was a lie. Edric is in the churchyard. He has been all along.
She puts the wooden ring on a string around her neck, and for the first time since you met her, she stands up straight.
You tell Ada that the women at the Willow Pool are asking for her.
She stares at you.
The Well Sisters? My mother used to go. I thought it had died out with her.
Something in her face loosens.
Washday. I'll go on washday.
She nods and goes back to turning the ring.
Ada looks up from the well.
The goblins on Collier's Trail. Are they still out there?
Of course he did. Stubborn fool. Two of them and a handcart.
She almost smiles. She presses ten copper into your hand and will not take it back. You receive 10 copper.
She closes her eyes.
Quick. Good. Thank you for not letting me imagine the rest.
Ada stands when she sees your face.
The goblins. On the trail. Are they…?
You tell her about Collier's Trail, and that nothing there will ever giggle again.
You tell her about the overturned handcart on Collier's Trail, the goblin arrows, and what Hobb carried back to Tobb.
She is quiet for a long time. She takes the knife and holds it against her chest.
And the ones who did it?
When you tell her they are dead, she sits back down on the well and cries until the bucket squeaks in the wind.
Goblins. He always said they never come out by day.
Her voice goes very flat.
Are they still there? On the trail?
Ada wants to know that Edric's killers are dead.
Her whole face lights up.
I knew it. He always said he'd sell the charcoal there. I'll wait.
She takes the coins without a word. Her eyes say she already knows.
Ada sees the knife in your hand before you say a word. Two letters are carved into the handle: E and A.
Ada sees the knife in your hand before you say a word. Two letters are carved into the handle: E and A.
Ada reads your face before you say a word.
Ada reads your face before you say a word.
You found him. Didn't you. Where is he?
Any news?
He took the handcart south from the crossroads, down Collier's Trail to the charcoal pits. Hobb the carter saw him turn onto it. Eight days ago now.
She grips your hand hard.
Thank you. Whatever it is, I would rather know. Folk say goblins have been seen on that trail. Be careful.
A young woman sits on the well's edge, turning a wooden ring over and over in her fingers.
My husband Edric took our handcart to the charcoal pits eight days ago, to buy charcoal for the winter. He hasn't come back.
Hobb the carter saw him at the crossroads, turning south onto Collier's Trail. That's the last anyone saw of him. You're armed. Would you look for him? Please.
He weeps openly.
I KNEW it. I'll write one about you next!
His lip trembles. Then he squares his shoulders.
Terrible… but memorable? I can work with memorable.
A patron of silence! That's a first.
He pockets the coins and immediately falls asleep.
A man with a lute and three feathers in his hat gapes at your ears.
An ELF! A real elf! You people invented music, didn't you? Then you must judge my new song! Ahem.
A man with a lute and three feathers in his hat blocks your way.
Friend! Judge my new song! Ahem.
Ohhh the goat, the goat, the goat went up the hill / and then the goat, the goat, the goat stood very still…
It continues for eleven verses. The goat never comes down.
Barnabas bites you on the way up and again on the way down. Wenna pinches your cheek and gives you a heel of bread and a coin. You receive 2 copper.
Barnabas bites you on the way up and again on the way down. Wenna pinches your cheek and gives you a heel of bread and a coin. You receive 2 copper.
Buy him? BUY Barnabas?
She thinks.
…Deal. He's yours. You'll regret it.
You hand him straight to Marta, who is delighted.
She looks at the goat. The goat looks at her.
…He does, doesn't he.
An old woman with a stick points furiously at the house roof. A goat stands on the thatch, chewing it thoughtfully. She squints at your ears.
Elf, are you? Good. You lot are supposed to be good with animals.
An old woman with a stick points furiously at the house roof. A goat stands on the thatch, chewing it thoughtfully.
That's Barnabas. Third time this week. He'll eat the whole roof and Hamond will blame me. Get him down, would you? Carefully, he bites.
Bless you. Bring a light. And maybe don't bring the ring, if you've got it.
He doesn't explain.
Tobb looks like he hasn't slept.
Something weeps in the yard at night. At Edric's grave. I've buried folk sixty years and never heard the dead complain.
The elder says it's owls. The elder doesn't sleep next to a graveyard. Come after dark, would you? See what it wants. I'll pay what I can.
Quiet as a church, last night. Here. Ten coppers, and I'll dig your grave for free when it's time. Not soon, I hope.
He hesitates, then hands you a bundle of black cloth.

Found this in the old crypt when I dug for Edric. A fen-woman's bodice, black and frayed, smelling of peat. Whoever she was, she was buried proud. Didn't feel right selling it. Feels right giving it to you.
You receive 10 copper and a Fen-Witch's Bodice.
Don't bring it back. Ever.
Tobb glances at the staff you carry, then at the pale woman's footprints by the gate.
Tobb glances at the staff you carry, then at the pale woman's footprints by the gate.
So you're learning from her. Hm.
He fetches something long wrapped in sacking.
Dug it out of the old ossuary, under the chapel. Bones bound to a yew pole. I've not slept right since it came in the house. Sixty coppers and it's yours, and good riddance.
An old man leans on his spade between the graves.
Quiet week. Nobody's died, and nobody's come back. That's how I like it.
He squints at the road.
Ada's man still not home? Collier's Trail's no place to be alone, these days.
You work until your hands blister. Tobb presses four coppers into your palm.
Don't argue.
You receive 4 copper.
The ring comes off easily. It is warm from the earth. Behind you, somewhere, a spade stops scraping. You receive 15 copper.
Tobb takes off his hood. For a while neither of you says anything.
Tobb takes off his hood. For a while neither of you says anything.
An old man leans on a spade beside a fresh mound of earth. The wooden marker reads EDRIC.
Hobb and I fetched him on a borrowed barrow, after you found him on Collier's Trail, poor lad. I buried him proper.
He lowers his voice.
He had a gold ring on him. I left it on. Sixty years digging, I never took a thing from the dead. My back though… my back's done. Help an old man finish the stones?
He listens, then spits into the fire.
Jaws like that in an honest wood. Good riddance.
He counts out coins, then stops and puts them back, and gives you more.
And this: watch the ground, not the beast. The ground tells you where it's going before it knows.
You receive 15 copper. (+1 agility, permanently)
He runs his thumb against the grain.
Old Greymaw. Twenty, and a fair price.
An afternoon of crawling through ferns.
Heel first. Then the outside of the foot. Breathe out when you step.
You come back filthy, scratched, and lighter on your feet than you have ever been. (+1 agility, permanently)
His face closes.
Jaw traps. Iron, big enough to take a man's leg. Somebody's been setting them on the Old Elven Road for the Baron's furriers.
I found an elf in one last spring, near dead. I'd break every one of them, but the man who sets them knows me.
He looks at you.
He doesn't know you.
Old Elven Road, past the Mistmere. Green hood, a bag of chains. He'll be checking his jaws at the west edge.
He pushes a stick of roast hare at you without looking up. The fire pops. Neither of you says much. Fully healed.
The pack follows an old grey brute the others call Greymaw. Kill him and the rest scatter. Go by day.
Deer are coming back. Give it a year.
A broad man in stained leather skins a hare by the fire. He looks at your ears, then at your quiet feet.
Elf. Thought I heard nothing coming.
A broad man in stained leather skins a hare by the fire. He nods at the log across the fire, which is as close to a welcome as you will get.
Brann looks up from his snares and nods.
Brann looks up from his snares and nods.
Ada is kneeling in the ploughed field, pressing seed into the furrows.
Ada is kneeling in the ploughed field, pressing seed into the furrows.
Holt leans against the fence, picking his teeth with a knife.
Mara says hello, friend. The village pays us too now. Funny how that works.
Guards! GUARDS!
He reads it twice. The colour leaves his face.
This… this is the Baron's own hand. Ordering murder. I was never here.
He runs, and his two soldiers run after him. You pull the stakes up one by one.
Written, you say? To the lords?
He pockets the coins and starts packing.
Measurements are so often wrong. Such a pity.
Sensible.
He drives in the last stake and hangs the Baron's banner from it. As he leaves, a paper slips from his satchel into the grass.
A thin clerk with ink-black fingers hammers a painted stake into the turf. Two soldiers in the Baron's colours lounge by the stones.
By order of Baron Bertram of Hollowmere, these boundary stones are hereby corrected. Dunhollow's common pasture now belongs to the Baron. Nothing personal. Just measurements.
She hands you a folded paper with a heavy red seal.
Took it off his man in grey, the night we left. His orders to burn us out, in his own hand. Do something useful with it.
You receive the Baron's Seal.
The pits are alive again: charcoal mounds smoking, children's laughter somewhere behind the kilns.
You let us go. So we came home instead of running. The Baron thinks we're gone. Let him think it.
Forty years I burned charcoal here. Then the Baron's men came with torches. Now…
He gestures at the smoke.
Now we burn it again. Thank you, stranger.
Behind you! The wolves first, then the trap!
The jaws bite your fingers before they give. Faelan drags his leg free and breathes for a while. Then he presses a silver leaf into your bloody hand.
Show this at the Silver Gate, north of the mere. They will know you as Faelan's friend.
You receive Faelan's Leaf.
He does not beg. He only watches you go, and says something soft in his own tongue that sounds like a name being written down. You take the Elven Blade.
Someone did,
he says.
And then they left.
A young elf lies in the reeds, one leg caught in an iron trap. The Baron's mark, a crude B, is stamped into its jaws. His face is grey with pain, but his eyes are sharp.
Kinsman? Here, among the axes? Then the stars have not forgotten me after all.
A human. Have you come to finish what the trap started, or to open it?
Walk in the light of the lanterns, kinsman. Sylvhaven is beyond the arch.
You carry Faelan's leaf. The gate is open to you, friend.
The axes are quiet. The gate remembers who quieted them. Pass.
He takes the leaf and holds it to the lantern. The silver warms, and for a moment the veins of it glow.
Faelan gave this to you himself. Then the gate already knows you. Keep it close: in Sylvhaven it speaks for you.
He takes the blade and turns it in the lantern light for a long while.
Faelan lived. He crawled home on his hands. He will not forgive you, and he should not. But a thief who comes back is rarer than a friend. Pass, and be watched.
The Fellings are quiet, and the birds went back to the silver trees. We saw who did it. Pass.
East of the mere, men of the Baron of Hollowmere are cutting down our silver trees and floating them south to sell. Each of those trees is older than your kingdom.
Stop the axes, and the gate will know your face.
He looks at the coins for a long time, as if they were a strange kind of beetle.
I have guarded this arch for three hundred years. What would I buy with that? A hat?
Behind him, the sentinel is trying not to laugh.
Two slender figures step out from between the white pillars. Their armour is made of gilded leaves, and their ears are long and pointed. Elves, out of the old stories.
Two slender figures step out from between the white pillars. Their armour is made of gilded leaves, and their ears are long and pointed. Elves, out of the old stories.
You carry the stink of the mere, and of Faelan's fear. The gate is closed to you.
We found one of ours in the reeds, too late. The wolves had him. Were you there? The mist says you were.
The gate stays shut.
No one of the short-lived has passed this arch in sixty years. Tell me why you should be the first.
Four thousand and twelve, four thousand and thirteen… leaves. I count them every spring. You made me lose my place.
Back to one, then.
He is leaning on a white staff, his leg bound in green cloth.
The healers say I will dance by midsummer. Badly. I always danced badly.
The Baron of Hollowmere sells our silver trees to shipwrights in the south. His axes are in the Fellings, east of the mere, and every day there are fewer songs in the wood.
We do not shed blood lightly. You have walked among the humans, and learned to. Stop the axes.
We do not shed blood lightly. Your kind does it every day, and sometimes well. Stop the axes.
Your pack is full. Make room, and come back.
It was made before your grandfather's grandfather was born. Wear it well.
You paid them to go. They will come back when the coin is spent, and bring their brothers.
She sighs.
Still, today the trees stand. Take this, for today.
You receive a Silver Circlet.
Choose a gift of Sylvhaven.
We heard the fighting from here. Blood in the Fellings. It will grow flowers, in time.
You drove them off with their own master's crimes. You have learned the humans' ways well.
You drove them off with their own master's crimes. That is a very human kind of wisdom.
You sent them to the colliers, to cut only dead wood. Clever. Even the old trees approve.
Then an envoy will walk with the next moon. If your village is kind, we will remember it for a thousand years. If it is not… we will remember that too.
Wise, and sad. Keep our secret, then. We will keep yours.
She is quiet for a long time.

Sixty years ago we stopped walking your roads. Your people burned a witch in Hollowmere, and we understood. If we come back, some will call us monsters. Some will call us gold. Tell me, which will Dunhollow do?
Aerwen, who keeps the lanterns of Sylvhaven. We are the last of the elves west of the mountains. The rest sailed, or sleep, or forgot us.
Your village and mine were friends once. The shrine in the mere remembers, even if nobody else does.
A tall woman in a white robe stands under the great silver tree. The light seems to come from her as much as from the lanterns.
By the fourth verse he is taking notes. By the ninth he is weeping.
Who wrote this? Pip? PIP? I must commission him. Take this to him.
He gives you twelve copper, which you do not give to Pip. You receive 12 copper.
He has to sit down.
In… pies.
He looks at the silver tree as if it has betrayed him by never mentioning this.
Mostly?
He brightens.
Then some of you are not. I will write a poem about the ones who are not.
A young elf with ink on his fingers seizes your sleeve.
One of us, who grew up among the humans! You must tell me everything. Is it true that they put cheese on bread? On purpose? And sing songs about animals?
A human! A real one! Tell me, is it true that your people put cheese on bread? On purpose? And sing songs about animals?
An old elf sits alone by the dead pool. The pavilions are black. The lanterns are glass and ash.
They came in the night, with torches and the Baron's banner. They knew the paths. Someone showed them the paths.
He does not look at you. He does not need to.
I felt it. The pool was bright for a moment, as bright as the evening she first came here, soaked to the knees, looking for her goat.
Thank you. I think I will go and sit with her awhile. Take my cloak; she always said it suited humans better.
You receive Calandor's elven cloak.
The moonbloom is not in your pack, and it is not in the ground. It is in a market somewhere.
He turns back to the water.
You have lived among the humans too long. You needed the coin more than the dead do.
Humans. You always need the coin more than the dead do.
The graveyard of Dunhollow, north of the well. Her name was Maren. Please.
He lifts a pale flower out of the water and holds it out to you.
Then lay this where she sleeps. If she sleeps.
You receive a Moonbloom.
I know,
I knew when I said it. It helps to hear it said by one of you.
An old elf sits by the moon pool, very still. Lily flowers glow on the water.
I had a friend in your village once. Maren, a weaver. She laughed like the brook. She said she would come back in the spring.
He smiles.
That was sixty springs ago.
You grew up among them. Perhaps you know how fast they count.
You short-lived people count so fast.
Our favourite guide! The Baron sends his thanks. The shipwrights send theirs. The elves, not so much.
He laughs until he coughs.
He reads, and swallows.
Murder. Of his own people. In his own hand.
He calls his men together.
Lads, we were never here. Leave the logs. Leave the axes if they're heavy.
Mara Blackthorn's back in the pits? And paying?
He scratches his beard.
Dead wood burns hotter anyway. And it doesn't sing at night.
He shivers.
These ones sing at night.
Thirty for a day off? You're a strange one.
They leave the logs where they lie.
His eyes go very small.
Elves. Real ones? With gold?
He counts out coins.
The Baron will make me a knight for this.
Pale stumps everywhere, like broken teeth. A heavyset man with a ledger looks up from a stack of silver-barked logs. Two men with axes stop chopping.
Pale stumps everywhere, like broken teeth. A heavyset man with a ledger looks up from a stack of silver-barked logs. Two men with axes stop chopping.
Silver-oak. Four gold a trunk from the shipwrights in Saltmouth. The Baron takes three, I take one, and the trees don't complain.
He squints at you.
Mostly they don't complain.
She is pressing silver seeds into the ground between the stumps.
In three hundred years this will be a forest again. Come back and see it.
She seems to mean it.
Dead wood only, the lad says. Grane's lads work harder than mine and complain less.
Something sings in those trees at night. Nobody cuts the live ones now.
A tall elf stands by the well, very patiently letting three children touch her ears.
Sylvhaven sends greetings to Dunhollow. Your elder has offered us bread. And cheese.
She looks deeply troubled.
Tirnel will be unbearable.
The old elf sits beside a small grey stone, a pale flower glowing on it.
She would have been eighty-four. I brought her the old songs. She liked the sad ones.
Let us see what you have.
(Only what is in your pack, not what you wear.)
Nothing in your pack I'd buy.
Let us see what you have.
Nothing in your pack I'd buy.
Let us see what you have.
Nothing in your pack I'd buy.
Let us see what you have.
Nothing in your pack I'd buy.
Your pack is full.
Your pack is full.
Your pack is full.
Your pack is full.
That's all I had today. Come back tomorrow.
That's all I had today. Come back tomorrow.
That's all I had today. Come back tomorrow.
That's all I had today. Come back tomorrow.
A man hugging a lamp post tells you, very seriously, that the lamp post is his best friend.
He never interrupts. Not like you.
You had not said anything.
THIEF!
A man with a cabbage in each hand points past you at a skinny hooded young woman with a loaf under her coat.
That's the third loaf this week! Grab her!
Psst. The crates behind the tannery. Nobody's watching them tonight. You didn't hear it from me.
Thanks for the bread.
She eats it very fast, like someone might take it back.
She stares at you like you grew a second head. Then she's gone into the crowd, bread and all.
The guard's glove closes on her shoulder. She doesn't cry. She just looks at you, and remembers you.
She grins, gap-toothed.
I owe you one, stranger.
And she vanishes, leaving Gerd yelling at the empty air.
The young woman clutches the loaf. She is all elbows and hunger, and her boots are two different boots.
It's for my brother. He's little. Please don't tell the guard.
The Crown's justice has come to Hollowmere. The statue will be recast as a horse trough. Everyone agrees this is an improvement.
…and by the grace of Baron Bertram the pasture of Dunhollow shall be improved by its annexation, for the good of the sheep, who are not consulted…
The Crown's justice has come to Hollowmere. The statue will be recast as a horse trough. Everyone agrees this is an improvement.
…and by the grace of Baron Bertram the pasture of Dunhollow shall be improved by its annexation, for the good of the sheep, who are not consulted…
The Baron's men took off their red and put on blue. Mostly the same men. Don't tell the Magistrate.
Keep walking. The Baron doesn't like crowds that aren't cheering.
The Baron's men took off their red and put on blue. Mostly the same men. Don't tell the Magistrate.
Keep walking. The Baron doesn't like crowds that aren't cheering.
I pay better than Marta. I also ask fewer questions.
Nothing to sell? Then stop blocking my light.
Pleasure. Don't read them in public.
You receive the Steward's Ledger.
She glances at the door, then pulls a folded bundle from inside her coat.
Pages cut out of the Steward's own ledger. What the Baron paid, and to whom. A clerk owed me money. Forty copper, and you never saw me.
Pleasure doing business.
Jory's crew? They jump everybody. It's a hobby.
Give me 15 copper and they'll leave you be. Or break their heads. Either way, keep it out of my shop.
A woman in green leather is sorting spoons that do not match.
The Crown's men are everywhere now. Bad for business. Good for sleep.
The Baron's taxes made thieves of half this ward. I just buy what the other half steals.
Wear it with pride. Rats can smell fear, and straw.
A thin man with a straw hat and a club inspects you for rats.
Tuck's the name, rats is the game. Rats in the tannery, rats in the keep, rats in the Baron's own bed! Well. One rat in the Baron's bed. The Baron.
He winks enormously.
An old woman holds a young man's arm as if he might blow away.
Tam came home! The logging crew in the east just… stopped. He says a stranger ended it.
She looks at you.
Was it you? Here. It's all I have.
You receive 6 copper.
An old woman sits in her doorway with a folded shirt in her lap.
My Tam went to cut trees for the Baron, east of the mere. They say there was a fight. They say… he isn't coming home.
You remember the loggers in the Fellings. You don't know which one was Tam.
An old woman sits in her doorway, mending by the last light.
My boy Tam went east with the Baron's loggers. Good money, they said. If you pass the Fellings, tell him his mother wants him home.
I'll never cut another tree. They sang, you know. At night. Mother thinks I'm mad.
He looks at his hands.
Maybe I am.
The Steward in the Castle Ward. Orrin. He keeps the Baron's secrets in his head and the Baron's money in his boots. Go careful.
A beggar with one eye and a very clean hat holds it out.
Spare a copper for a veteran of the Baron's wars? Which wars, you ask? All of them. He loses them all.
A broad woman behind the bar is pulling a pint with one hand and throwing out a drunk with the other.
You know my cousin Pip? The one with the goat song?
He shudders.
The family doesn't talk about the goat song.
A lutenist plays something sad and very good. When you ask, he says his cousin Pip in Dunhollow is the talented one. He is lying.
An old priestess sweeps the chapel steps.
The bells rang for an hour when they took the Baron. I didn't ring them. I don't know who did.
The Magistrate from the Crown sleeps in our guest room. He is a patient man. He is waiting for someone to bring him the truth.
The keep's sealed for the trial. Nobody in or out.
The Baron sees no one without the Steward's leave. Talk to Orrin.
The keep's sealed for the trial. Nobody in or out.
The Baron sees no one without the Steward's leave. Talk to Orrin.
Our loyal friend from Dunhollow! The Baron sleeps better thanks to you. Come back if you find anything else… inconvenient.
He tucks the paper into his boot without reading it.
Wise. Very wise. The Baron remembers his friends.
The coins are heavy and warm. You receive 60 copper.
Want? Nothing. The Baron wants what every lord wants: more. More pasture, more timber, more tolls.
He smiles thinly.
Dunhollow sits on good land and pays little tax. That is a problem the Baron is solving. Slowly. Legally, where possible.
A lean man in bright mail and a red surcoat looks you over as if pricing you.
So you are the one who chased our surveyor off the boundary stones. The Baron has heard of you. He is… interested.
A traveller from the south road. From Dunhollow, by the mud. What brings you to the Baron's door?
The trial begins at the next assize. The Crown thanks you. The valley, I suspect, will thank you longer.
He reads it once, and then again, with his lips pressed white.
By morning the red banners are down. The Baron of Hollowmere is arrested.
By morning the red banners are down. The Baron of Hollowmere is arrested.
Murder of his own subjects, in his own hand, under his own seal.
His steward's letters. Bribes, threats, a list of names. The Keep's own hand.
The Keep paid trappers to snare the King's free elves. That alone is treason.
The Steward's own ledger: every copper paid to Mara's cutthroats.
Mara Blackthorn's journal. Dates, coin, and whose coin it was.
Guard! Wake the Crown's men. We go to the keep tonight.
He breaks nothing and hurries nothing. He reads the charter by the window, twice, then holds the lead seal up to the light.
The old king's grant. Genuine.
He looks at you properly for the first time.
Then the Baron's surveyors are forgers, and his new pasture is theft from the Crown's own grant. That is enough to open an inquiry. It is not enough to hang him.

West end of the pond, by the old bones. Don't let it get behind you.

And it stank of smoke!

Why?

Find me in the Gate Ward. Aldo pays his debts. Usually with interest, which is more than the bank does.
Five coppers. I'll buy a very small blanket.
He waddles off toward the city.
Oh yes, hilarious. I'll remember that face.

Highwaymen! Took my cart, my purse, my coat, my shirt, my boots, and my dignity. They left the hose. Out of pity, I think.
I'm Aldo. I sell cloth in Hollowmere. Or I did, when I had cloth.
My benefactor! People ask why I'm wearing your shirt under all this. I tell them it's lucky.
The blanket was very small. But it was a blanket.
Aldo, fully dressed and then some, grabs your hand.
You! The shirt! Here, twenty copper, and a proper tunic. Madder-red, my best.
Also, the highwaymen. They work the King's Road after dark, and the toll-keeper looks the other way. Now you know why.

Five coppers, returned with interest. Eight! I'm a man of business.

laughed at me

Ithilwen sits on the warm stones, drying in the moonlight as if clothes were a human idea.
Watcher! The water is still singing. Go in, we'll keep the road.

The watcher on the road! The trappers have not come back. Bathe with us, friend, and let us keep watch this time.
Back again? The moon remembers you.
A scarred woman in a dented breastplate.
I've kept this town from burning for eleven years, under a man I despised. Half my guards haven't been paid since the arrest. They're turning to the road already.
Give me the town, and I'll have order in a week. Curfew, patrols, and a rope for anyone who robs a traveller.
The Baron's steward, pale and manacled, still somehow neat.
I kept his books. I know where every copper went, which means I know where every copper is. Nobody else does.
Pardon me and I'll run it clean. Taxes stay; the treasury is empty, and the roads and the well and the guards do not pay for themselves.
And there'd be something in it for you. Thirty copper, for the recommendation.
A round man in very good wool.
Let the guilds govern! Free trade, low tolls, a council of honest merchants. The market will flourish.
He does not mention the Lowstreets. When you ask, he says
the market will lift everyone,
and looks at his rings.
Order. It's what people ask for, until they have it.
He writes.
The roads will be safe within the week. I hope the rope stays in its drawer.
Aldous reads it, then reads it again.
Elf-silver. And ears.
He looks across the chapel at the manacled steward, who has gone the colour of candle wax.
Steward Orrin will be standing trial beside his master. Thank you. That leaves two.
The Baron's own steward.
A long look.
Competent, I grant. Crooked, I suspect. You'll forgive me if I count the silver in the chapel.
Later a boy in grey slips you a purse. You receive 30 copper. Prices in Hollowmere will stay high.

Merchants. Well, they'll keep the lights on, if only in the Market Ward.
He writes. Prices in Hollowmere will fall; rents, perhaps, will not.
Aldous looks older than he did.
The Baron is in chains. Good. And now nobody is collecting taxes, nobody is paying the guard, and three people have been in my chapel since dawn, each explaining why the town should be theirs.
The Crown will appoint whoever I recommend. I am a stranger here. You are not, quite. So: whom?
He weighs the purse.
From you. Not the Crown, not the town. You.
He shakes his head.
The lads will go home. Me, I've none. Does your village need a watchman?
Wise.
He steps aside. Behind you, later, you hear a cart stop, and a woman shouting.
Blackthorn? We burned her people out of the Pits.
…And she'd take us?
She took me in,
says the youngest deserter quietly,
before I signed on with the Baron.
Harl looks at him for a long time. Then they go east.

Toll,

Hamond needed a watch. Turns out I needed a village. Nobody's robbed on the forest road while I'm awake, and I sleep very little.
You lower yourself into water hot enough to cook a turnip. Every ache in you gives up at once.
Across the steam, the other bathers pick up their gossip where they left it. You are fully healed.
A broad woman with steam-reddened arms and a voice that fills the cellar.
Three coppers for the hot water, one for a towel, nothing for the gossip. Clothes on the hook, modesty at the door. Nobody looks here, and if they do, I throw them out.

You caught him! He's been rolling sixes on me since midsummer.
She leans close.
Watch his left hand when he's losing. That's all I'll say.
Paid? Ha. I'm guarding my own bed so nobody steals it.

Our carter broke an axle in the Gate Ward this morning, by the inn yard, and ran off to find a wheelwright. Two sacks are still on the cart. Fetch them before the gate guards find them first. Mira will write you into the book.
A man in a black beret and a gold-braided waistcoat leans on the post under the Company's black banner, a ledger the size of a door under one arm and a hammer through his sash.
Alaric Craban, Ratsherr of the Gold Brothers Trading Company. We buy, we sell, we ship out of Port Fearn Arianhod, and we never forget a debt, in either direction.
Every great house starts the same way: two sacks of fourage and twenty gold. We've got the gold. Bring me two sacks of fourage and you've got work.
Twenty gold. Well: ten copper, the gold is a figure of speech. Mira! Write them in. Associate of the Company.
He taps the ledger.
And now I have real work for you.
You drop two sacks at his feet. Craban opens one, sniffs it, and actually smiles.
Good. Look in the ditches on the west side, below the second milestone. Robbers hide what they can't carry.

One of our wagons went missing on the King's Road, south of the gallows. Driver ran home without it. The wagon's gone but the strongbox wasn't on it when it was found, so someone's hidden it, or dropped it.
Find the box. Don't open it. That's important. Don't open it.
The box, Associate. West ditch, King's Road.
He looks at the bracelets for a long time.
The Company never forgets a debt. Even one it didn't know it owed.
He pushes them to you.
Take them to the elves at the Silver Gate. Tell them the Gold Brothers want no part of this. And tell them we'd like to trade honestly, if they'll have us.
You receive 15 copper and Three Elven Bracelets.
Business is business.
He says it the way you'd say a prayer you don't believe.
Your share. Thirty.
You receive 30 copper. He closes the box and does not look at it again.
Your hand is faster than his eyes. Probably. He counts the coin, not the silver.
Fifteen for your trouble.
You receive 15 copper.
Through the open door, Mira Quell looks up from her ledger, and then down again.
You set the strongbox down on the cobbles. Craban's eyes go straight to the split in the lid, and the silver glinting through it.
You looked.
Not a question. He opens it: coin, papers, and three silver bracelets wrapped in a receipt signed O.
Elven work. Bought from the Keep's steward.
He is quiet for a moment.
I didn't order these. Someone in Port Fearn did, on the Company's account. They'd fetch a fortune across the sea.
The Silver Gate, Associate. North of the Mistmere. The bracelets won't walk there on their own.
Craban doesn't look up.
Mira checked the manifest. Three bracelets. I received two.
The Company never forgets a debt. We'll still buy what you sell. Don't ask us for anything else.
Welcome aboard, in spirit. Come back in three days.
The Company's sending a ship to Port Fearn Arianhod. Every Associate may buy a share. Fifty copper in, and in a few days, we'll see what the sea gives back.
And since your elves opened their road to us, the hold will carry silverleaf cloth. Honestly bought.
Wool and fourage out, spice and cloth back. Unless the Crown's inspectors take an interest.
The ship's still out. The sea doesn't hurry.
Craban looks grey.
The Crown's inspectors boarded her at the river mouth. They were looking for anything Steward Orrin had sold. They found the bracelets.
Ship, cargo, shares. All of it.
He doesn't blame you out loud. He doesn't have to.
Craban is grinning.
She came home heavy!
Silverleaf cloth, bought from the elves at the Gate. The merchants of Port Fearn fought over it. Your share, Partner.
Spice and dye. A good season. Your share, Partner.
Partner! The next ship sails at midsummer. There's always a next ship.
We'll build it back. Two sacks of fourage and twenty gold, remember?
She closes the book before you can read the rest.
Mind you don't spill anything on it. Alaric would have both our heads.
A precise young woman with ink on every finger.
The Company's ledger. If you're not in it, you don't exist, commercially speaking.
You hold out the three bracelets and tell the warden where they came from: the trappers, the steward, the ship's hold, and a merchant who chose to send them home.
The warden takes them as if they were alive.
These were Ilmarë's. She did not come back from the reeds.
Tell your merchant the Silver Gate remembers honest men. He may send a wagon.
A barrel-chested man with the Company's crossed bars tattooed on his forearm, ticking crates off a list.
Any friend of Alaric's drinks free on my deck.
Looking for work? The Gold Brothers' counting house is in the Market Ward. Tell Craban that Bram sent you.
Your pack's full. Come back when you've got room for opportunity.
Sella. Not the guard, not the priest, not your mother. Sella.
A lean man in a green hood watches the river as if he expects it to pay him.
You've got an honest face. Terrible thing, in this town.
He produces a package sealed in black wax.
Carry this to Sella in the Lowstreets. Don't open it. Thirty copper when she has it.
Sella's in the Lowstreets. The one with the key over the door. Why are you still here?
Tomas tips his hood.
Good courier. Rare as honest bread.
Tomas looks at you the way the river looks at a stone.

She drops it straight into the brazier behind her. Black wax, paper, gone.

Sella's eyes go to the black wax before they go to you.
Tomas's. Unopened?
She checks the seal with a fingernail.
Unopened. How refreshing.
Don't touch it with gold on your hands. I'm not joking. Well. I'm mostly not joking.
A younger man with his brother's jaw and none of his patience, watching the Golden Fourage as if it might leave without him.
Ruvin Craban. Alaric keeps the books; I keep the ships and go where the maps run out. Shrines, caves, one very disappointing dragon egg.
You're in the ledger, so I'll speak plainly. Goblins north of the Wolfwood have dug into a cave that glows green. I've seen crystal like that once before. Bring me a shard.
Get yourself into my brother's ledger first. Then we'll talk about caves.
The goblins' cave. North of the Wolfwood. Green light. You can't miss it, which is the problem.
Twenty, and a berth on the next ship that sails for Port Fearn Arianhod. When she sails. Alaric will pretend he agreed to it.
Twenty copper. And my thanks, which is rarer.

I don't believe in her. I just don't wear gold near the crystal.
He holds the shard up to the light. It hums. The coins in his purse clink, all by themselves.
Same as the cave in the east. So it's true.
The crystal sits in a lead box in my cabin. It still hums. I sleep in the hold now.
Partner. When the ship sails for Port Fearn, there's a berth with your name on it.
Alaric says hello. He doesn't, but he means it.
The straw is fresh and the blanket smells of smoke. You sleep like the dead, which in Dunhollow is saying something. You are fully healed.
A big woman polishing a cup that will never be clean.

Maren the weaver? Lord, that's a name. She went up to the mere every spring when I was a boy, and came back singing. Folk said she had an elf for a sweetheart.

Died the winter I turned twelve.

B. Bertram. Baron Bertram of Hollowmere. He has wanted the land below the old boundary stones since my father's day. So now he sends cutthroats to bleed the farms and pay his way in.
You did well to bring this to me. Take this for your trouble, it is not much. And keep that letter safe. One day someone above him may need to read it.

There is a wood north of the crossroads: through the Ridge Tunnel west of the village, then along the Mill Track. Wolves have taken to it this spring, led by a grizzled old brute the hunters call Greymaw. We have lost two sheep and nearly a child.
Clear them out and the village will pay you what it can.
The wood lies north of the crossroads. Take the tunnel west out of the village, then the Mill Track. Follow the arrow with the wolf's head scratched into it.
Greymaw too? Then the shepherds will sleep tonight.
He counts a few coins out of a worn purse and presses them into your hand.
It is not much, but it is what the village can spare. Marta will give you a fair price for that pelt, too.
South of the crossroads, where the old charcoal burners worked. Smoke rises there most nights now. A woman named Mara Blackthorn leads them, they say.
Break that camp and Bertram loses his hands in this valley. The village will pay you for it.
Work? Bandits have been bleeding the farms along the forest road. Yours too, by the look of you.
Gone? Not dead, but gone?
He strokes his beard.
Mercy is a strange coin. But the road is ours.
Mara Blackthorn beaten? Then the road is ours again.
He counts out coins with shaking hands.
He looks at your full purse for a long time.
I see.

Tobb says there are men at the old boundary stones, north past the graveyard. Baron's men, with stakes and a clerk.
My father said those stones were raised when the old king gave this valley to the people who farm it. If they move, our sheep have nowhere to graze, and Bertram has his pasture at last.
I have had the path past the graveyard untied for you. I cannot ask more of you. But I am asking.
North past the graveyard. Tobb will show you the path.
A charter? My grandmother swore there was one. I thought it was a story for children.
Ask Old Wenna. She is the only one old enough to remember the stories properly. She'll be by her goat.
Dig at night, beside the stones? Well. Take a spade and do not tell Tobb.
He unrolls the lead-sealed parchment with hands that do not shake at all. For a long moment he only reads.
…to the free folk of the hollow, the land below the stones, for as long as the stones stand.
He laughs, once, very loud.
For as long as the stones stand! And you kept them standing.
Then, quieter:
Well. Where they stood. The charter says where, and Bertram's stakes do not.

This is not for my strongbox. This is for the Crown. There is a magistrate of the King in Hollowmere, they say, asking questions. Take it to him. I have written a letter of passage: the gate guard will let you in with it.
You receive 25 copper. Hamond's letter will open the gate of Hollowmere.
Dunhollow is thirty souls, a well, and more sheep than sense. We sit at the top of the lane, where the forest road meets the old trade way. That was a blessing once.
Marta keeps the stall by the barrels. If you have coin, or things worth coin, she will deal.
Marta looks at your ears for a very long time.
Marta looks at your ears for a very long time.
My grandmother said elves pay in moonlight and leaves. You'll pay in copper, same as everyone. …Can I touch them? No? Fair.
Three wolf pups tumble around Marta's boots.
My favourite customer! For you, a friend's price.
Barnabas the goat is eating Marta's awning. She doesn't seem to mind.
For Barnabas's hero, a discount!
Good day! Steel, leather, a hat for your head. And if you have things to sell, I will look at them.
Heavy for its size, sealed in black wax stamped with a plain O.
You could break the seal. It would be obvious that you had.
Her friends burn. Frost will slow them. Or simply hit them very hard.
My apprentice, Tessaly, took my starwood staff and ran. She has found others who think fire is an argument. They are in the Drowned Shrine, past the Mistmere.
I came down from Hollowmere after her. I am too old to wade through a fen and too proud to ask the Baron's men.
Bring her back. Or bring the staff back. I will not pretend I know which matters more to me.
She is sitting by the fire pretending not to listen. We go home when you have finished your lessons. She hates me. She is studying again. Both of those are progress.
She is in the tower. She hates me. She is studying again. Both of those are progress.
You tell him how you got it. He listens to all of it.
You beat a frightened girl in a swamp for a stick.
He turns back to his books.
Keep it. I find I do not want it any more. And do not ask me to teach you anything again.
He looks at you a long time.
Then she chose. I suppose I should have let her choose sooner.
An old man in a travel-stained blue robe sits over a cup of Bertha's cider he has not touched. A staff with a faintly glowing blue stone leans on the bench beside him.
An old man in a pale robe leans on a staff topped with a stone that glows faintly blue.
Ah. The one who brought her home.
A wanderer. You have the look of someone who hits things. Have you ever considered hitting them from further away?
She lets the staff drop.
Fine. But I'm telling him to his face.
Later, Orvell pays you twenty-five copper and does not look at you. You receive 25 copper.
She stares at you. Then she presses the staff into your hands.
Take it. It was always his. I'll make my own.
She is gone into the mist before you can answer. You receive the Starwood Staff.
The stone in the staff flares white. Her knuckles go white with it.
Take it, then. If you can.
A young woman in a scorched robe stands in the ruined shrine, her master's starwood staff in her hands. Her friends lie in the reeds.
He sent you. Of course he did. Did he tell you he burned my notes? That he said I would never be more than his servant with a stick?
The young woman at the altar grips her master's starwood staff and steps back behind her friends.
Orvell's dog. Talk to them first.
A goblin sits on an enormous sack.
Everything free! 0 gold, 0 silver, 0 copper! Gratis sells to anyone, even big-folk.
Pip leaps onto a table, nearly falls off it, and strikes a chord that makes Bertha wince.
THE BALLAD OF THE WANDERER! Verse the first!
The tavern applauds, mostly out of relief.

My muse! Sit, sit. I've added verses.

I could. I need two things I do not have.
Moonthread, spun from the light on Nimuë's pool. Ask her at night, when the moon is on the water.
And a setting of plain silver, made by a hand that does not tremble. The armourer in Hollowmere is said to be good, for a human.
Her needle stops. She is looking at the coin in your hand.
Moonsilver. Where did a human find that? No, do not tell me. The moon gives it to whom she likes.
Loose in a pocket it is only cold. Set right, it would sharpen every spell you cast, and make your feet lighter besides. A focus.

A rope is tied across the path north, hung with a sign: By order of the Baron. Keep out. Tobb shrugs.
Baron's men up at the old stones. Hamond's the one to ask about it, not me.

Cleared. Took us long enough. The causeway runs on into the Drowning Fen. I wouldn't go. Old Morwen lives out there, and worse than Morwen.
The Drowning Fen. Used to be fields, my grandad said, before the water came up. There's a woman lives out there in a hut on legs. And things in the mud that aren't frogs.
He hits the trunk. Chock.
Treasure too, folk say. Folk say a lot.
He looks at the trunk, then at you.
See that? That's a scratch. We've barely started.
Halfway, near enough. The crown's off, the root's the swine.
Few more days. The last big section's always the worst.
You've got the whole valley to help, by the sound of it. Go do that. Word gets round when we're through.
A broad man with an axe and a beard full of sawdust doesn't stop swinging while he talks.
Mind the chips! Biggest oak in the valley, came down in the spring storm, right across the causeway. Can't go round: it's bog on both sides, and the bog eats folk.
We're taking it apart a log at a time. It'll be done when it's done. Come back in a while.
The causeway's shut till we're done. Ask Gerd.

The heart of the Weighing Stones. Goblins sat on this for a hundred years and used it to keep their soup warm.
He sounds personally offended.
I can set it in a staff. It will take my best ash-wood and an afternoon, and forty copper for the wood.
South, he said. Past the old woman's hut. Bring him back by the ear if you have to.
Gerd is pacing by the cart, axe forgotten in his hand.
Gerd is pacing by the cart, axe forgotten in his hand.
We cleared the oak, and that idiot boy Pim went straight into the fen. Said he saw lights. Pretty lights, he said, going south.
Nobody follows lights in the Drowning Fen. Nobody comes back from following them, mostly. Find him? I'll pay what the crew can scrape.
Pim is on the cart under three blankets, shivering and sweating at once. Ulla has stopped shouting at him.
Pim is on the cart under three blankets, shivering and sweating at once. Ulla has stopped shouting at him.
Fen-fever. The bog gets into you.
Gerd looks older.
Gisla, the herb-wife on the Mill Track, brews a warm tonic for it. If anyone has one, she does.
Gisla's warm tonic. Mill Track, west of Dunhollow. He's getting worse.
You tip Gisla's tonic into Pim. He makes a face like a drowned cat, sweats it out, and by evening is sitting up and being shouted at by Ulla again.
Gerd grips your hand.
Fifteen copper from the crew, and my old felling axe. It's taken down bigger things than that oak.
You receive 15 copper and a Felling Axe.
No sign of him? South. The Sunken Hollow, probably. The lights go there.
He wades out after you, still looking back over his shoulder at the reeds.
Pim is standing knee-deep in the mud, staring at the reeds by the old stones with his mouth open.
Pim is standing knee-deep in the mud, staring at the reeds by the old stones with his mouth open.
They go in there! The lights! Into the reeds, and then they're gone. There's a door, I swear there's a door behind them.
He finally looks at you.
…Is Gerd angry?
First lesson: listen. Three graves here have something left undone, and the dead do not talk to strangers with empty hands.

Maren the weaver, by the east wall, never finished her blue cloth. Bertha at the Wheatsheaf still has her last spool. Gerrit the miller, under the yew, fed this village forty years and nobody ever thanked him: take him a loaf. And the one by the west wall has no name at all. Old Wenna was alive the fever winter. Ask her.
Then come at night, sit with each of them, and keep still until the light has finished speaking. One night will do, if you have done the asking.
A pale woman in a black robe leans on a staff very like the hedge-witch's. Up close, she smells of rain and turned earth.
The dead talk all the time. Nobody listens. That is the whole craft, really: listening, and then asking very politely for something back.
Any fool with a black staff can Drain, Wither and Raise: the staff knows those words by itself. The dead can teach you better ones. If you are willing to listen.
Maren wants her blue spool: Bertha has it. Gerrit wants a loaf, and a thank-you. The nameless one wants her name: Old Wenna knows it. Then sit with them at night, and keep still.
Vesna looks at you for a long moment.
You stayed. Most people get up and leave when the dead start talking about themselves.

Feel that, round your ankles? They held on to you while you sat. The dead do that, when they like you. That is Grave Grasp: hands from the earth that hold your foe fast, mid-swing or not. Put it in your spellbook.
The second word is ugly, so it is taught by an ugly teacher. There is a gallows on the King's Road. The man on it has been dead nine years and is still complaining about it.
Go at night and cut him down. Bring me his bones, and three more from men who died badly: there are plenty of those on the roads, and they do not need them. We will put him somewhere better.
The gallows on the King's Road. At night, when he is talkative. Cut him down.
Tobb fills the hole himself, and mutters something that might be a prayer. On the King's Road that night, the rope stops creaking.
Tobb fills the hole himself, and mutters something that might be a prayer. On the King's Road that night, the rope stops creaking.
Vesna hands you the skull without comment. It is surprisingly light.
Vesna hands you the skull without comment. It is surprisingly light.
He will not like that. You may hear about it, on the road, at night.
Vesna lays the bones out on the grass, the hanged man's in the middle, the three others round him like a fence.
Vesna lays the bones out on the grass, the hanged man's in the middle, the three others round him like a fence.
Now watch.
She snaps the hanged man's thigh-bone across her knee, and the splinter flies from her hand straight through the fence post behind you.
Bone Spear. Old bone is the hardest thing there is: shields and wards do not stop it. Put it in your spellbook.
Now. Tobb has a hole ready. Or you can keep his skull. Some of us like a keepsake.
The last lesson is about the risen. You can raise them; any staff can. But they will not die for you until one of the dead has shown you how.

Under this yard is the old crypt. I have the key; Tobb thinks it is lost. Below, there is a man called Corran who has wanted to lie down properly for two hundred years, but the bone-gates will not open for the living.
So you will wake him, and he will follow you, and every gate you bring him to will know its own. Get him to the bottom. Keep the restless ones off him.
The crypt, at the back of the yard. Corran is waiting for you just inside. Walk slowly: he is old.

That is all I have. The fen has older dead than these, if you want to see what the words can do: a hag who stole my lantern, and a drowned king under the reeds. Use it kindly. Or at least on people who deserve it.
Vesna puts her hand on your arm. Her fingers are cold.
You felt him stand, didn't you, when you came near him? And lie down again when you brought him home.

He knelt for you. Bones remember who they stood for. Now, when your risen one stands beside you, call it again, and it will throw itself between you and the blow. Bone Shield. It costs you the skeleton. It is worth it.
The fen is quieter since you came. I don't know if that is good.
The dead are quieter since you came. They have someone to talk to.
She holds it in the heart of the forge with her bare hand until the rust runs off it like water. What she gives back is grey and clean and still warm.
Your witch can have it now.
Ilka's eyes go to the rusted blade before they go to you.

Give it here. Fire does in a breath what a grindstone does in a day.
Ilka watches the Emberbrand at your side the way a mother watches a child cross a river.

It drinks from both wells, that one: the strength of your arm and the fire you carry. Feed both and it will never fail you.
The Flamesworn captain stole a blade from me. Bring it back, and three ember cores from the pass, and I will wake what sleeps in it.
Ilka takes the Fire Blade and the three cores and lays them in the heart of the forge. The cores melt into the steel like butter.

She hammers once, twice, and the whole valley seems to ring. When she lifts it out, the blade is dark as old glass, and fire runs along its edge.
The Emberbrand. Your arm swings it. Your spells feed its flame. And whatever it cuts will burn.
Maelis lets the loom run on by itself and looks you over, piece by piece, the way a tailor would.
Maelis lets the loom run on by itself and looks you over, piece by piece, the way a tailor would.
Each thing you wear can hold one thread of moonlight, no more. Choose well. The thread is not cheap, and finer cloth takes a finer thread.
Come back wearing something. I cannot weave into skin.
Your crate's the biggest one in the cellar already. Any bigger and I'd be renting you the cellar.
Vesna watches your last skeleton fall apart in the reeds and tilts her head.

They punch. Did you notice? Bones remember how to stand, but they have forgotten how to hold anything. The dead let go of everything, first of all their weapons.

Watch how they hold their blades as they fall. Then come back, and I will show you how to put a weapon back in a dead hand.
Pick something with a bit of style. They have been lying in the dark a long time.
Vesna takes your hand and closes your fingers around nothing, as if around a hilt. Her hand is very cold.

There. That is how they held them. Now, when you carry a grave-speaker's staff, you can give the dead you raise a weapon of your own choosing. It will not make them hit any harder. The dead do not care about steel. But they look the part, and that matters more than you'd think.
She breathes on the glass and the flame steadies, warm and gold. She puts the lantern back in your hands.
Keep it. It burns green near the dead and gold near the living, and it will light your road when the sun is gone. Two of my draughts and a little coin besides. The rest you'll have to dig for.
You receive 15 copper and two healing draughts. Vesna's Lantern is yours: carry it in your off hand (+2 Spell Power, +2 Attack Power, light at night).
Vesna takes the lantern in both hands and holds it up to her face. The little flame inside turns green, then gold.
